source.title: Transformers Use Causal World Models in Maze-Solving Tasks
source.authors: Alex F Spies; William Edwards; M. I. Ivanitskiy; Adrians Skapars; Tilman Rauker; Katsumi Inoue; Alessandra Russo; M. Shanahan

record.file_problem: Whole paper is present. The text has minor extraction and layout artifacts, but the relevant sections and tables are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper does not reproduce Toy Models of Superposition or test feature-over-capacity geometry. It does test aspects of SAE feature completeness and stability in maze-solving transformers, and reports whether connection representations use one or multiple SAE features.
record.gate_note: The paper cites superposition as motivation for using SAEs, but does not test the original toy-model claim about sparse features, overlap geometry, or sparsity-dependent transitions. SAE reconstruction and a second SAE on Stan bear on V5. The reported one-feature versus compositional codes bear on V6. Intervention efficacy results are not recorded as V5 rows because they measure perturbation effects, not whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical.
record.test_reason: A borderline case: SAEs are mainly a tool here, but the paper reports completeness (reconstruction and behaviour preservation) and a second-SAE stability check that bear on V5. Terry's single-feature connection code bears weakly on V6. The setting is new: two 6-layer maze-solving transformers. Nothing bears on V1–V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but incomplete. The authors conclude that maze transformers form causal world models whose connection codes differ by positional encoding: single features in Terry, a compositional code in Stan. They also conclude that activating features works better than removing them, and that Stan can handle extra connections added in SAE latent space even though it fails on the equivalent longer inputs. They treat SAE reconstruction as evidence of completeness.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses SAE feature discovery and causal interventions in maze-solving transformers; it does not reproduce Toy Models of Superposition's toy-network setup or its feature-geometry and sparsity measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The representation differs between the learned-position-embedding model Stan and the rotary-position-embedding model Terry.

fits_no_version.finding: Stan's connection code combines a connection-specific feature with a generic semicolon feature shared across connections. The authors attribute this to positional information being entangled with the world model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How a feature is decomposed by an SAE (single vs compositional latents) depends on architecture choices such as the positional-encoding scheme.

record.problems: Evidence for V5 is limited to two maze-task transformers; the additional-SAE stability comparison is reported only for Stan. The paper does not establish cross-model or cross-task canonicality, and does not report uncertainty estimates for these measurements.
record.rows_left_out: Intervention efficacy results in Figure 9 and Figure 19 were not included because they measure the effects of toggling SAE features, rather than SAE reconstruction completeness, stability, or the number of features used to encode a connection.

untested.parts: Not tested: no toy model, no sparsity sweep, no feature-geometry measurement.
Not tested: no capacity or importance manipulation.
Not tested: neuron polysemanticity is not studied.
Not tested: no LLMs are studied.
Untested: canonicality across training runs, models or tasks; stability for Terry; stability of features beyond the connection features.
Untested: no search for or test of multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: The predominant SAE features in both models are distributed and hard to interpret; the authors say they may be suppressed by higher sparsity penalties. This bears on whether SAE features are clean units and on their dependence on the sparsity penalty.
Zero-patched token error as a control: Terry 8.52 vs 8.18 unperturbed; Stan 8.61 vs 6.35. Terry's small gap weakens the completeness contrast.

record.verdict_notes: Table 3 headers and values are misaligned in the extracted text. The reading used here puts L2, L1 and L0 first, then the three patched columns. Only under this reading does SAE-patched equal unperturbed exactly, which matches the caption. Intervention efficacy (Figs. 9, 19) was rightly left out. The paper is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not vary feature count relative to dimensions, feature sparsity or importance, or measure overlapping near-orthogonal feature geometry or a transition.
It does not test whether polysemanticity arises from competition for limited capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
It does not study polysemantic neurons or alternative causes of polysemanticity.
The studied systems are maze-task transformers, not LLMs; the study does not test feature spreading across LLM neurons or SAE recovery of LLM features.
It evaluates SAE reconstruction behavior and reports a second-SAE result for Stan, but does not establish that SAE features are canonical across training runs, architectures, or tasks.
It compares single-feature and compositional SAE codes for maze connections, but does not test the dimensionality of superposed features in the original toy-model sense.

rows.subject: Stan
rows.operation_detail: Decoded maze-connection presence from SAE features and inspected the code used for each connection.
rows.measure: Number and arrangement of SAE features encoding a connection
rows.value: Two features per connection: a connection-specific feature and a more generic semicolon feature
rows.note: The authors describe this as a compositional code; the generic feature appears across connections.
rows.check: The code is two 1-D SAE latents, one of them a generic semicolon feature shared by all connections. That is a composition of 1-D directions, not an irreducible multi-dimensional feature, so it can't show V6 failing. The V5 link is dropped because the row measures code structure, not completeness or stability.

rows.subject: Terry
rows.operation_detail: Decoded maze-connection presence from SAE features and inspected the code used for each connection.
rows.measure: Number and arrangement of SAE features encoding a connection
rows.value: A single SAE feature for each connection; the authors describe it as a single direction in the residual stream
rows.note: The authors describe connection information as cleanly encoded in single features.
rows.check: This is weak evidence: the SAE can only recover 1-D directions, so one latent decoding a connection near-perfectly (Fig. 15a) is consistent with V6 but does not test it against a multi-dimensional alternative. The V5 link is dropped.

labels.reason: Section 3.2 explicitly identifies individual connection features with single residual-stream directions; Figure 15a supports single-latent decoding. This is weak, local support because no multidimensional alternative is tested.

relation.reason: Although SAEs are primarily an analysis tool, the paper's own reconstruction and replication results bear on V5, and Terry's single-direction connection code bears weakly on V6.

tranche.reason: A new maze-transformer setting reports reconstruction fidelity, behavior preservation, replication of Stan's connection code, and directional connection features.

source_check.notes: Table 3 has six metric columns with recoverable assignments; R1–R4 confuse these columns. R5–R6 restate behavior-preservation evidence rather than independent evaluations; R9 establishes replication of a code structure, not canonical feature identities.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Terry and Stan, analyzed SAE reconstructions
reader_labels.reason: The authors report low token reconstruction errors and no effect on model behavior from replacing activations with SAE reconstructions (R1–R6). The additional SAE for Stan reproduced its compositional code (R9). These results support completeness and within-model stability in the tested settings, not canonicality in general.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Each maze connection was encoded by one SAE feature, described by the authors as a single residual-stream direction (R8).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Stan represented each connection compositionally with a connection-specific feature plus a generic semicolon feature, rather than with one feature per connection (R7).
